title: How to Tell if an Egg Is Bad: Reliable Signs and the Float Test

seo.title: How to Tell if an Egg Is Bad
seo.meta_description: A rotten odor after cracking is the clearest spoilage sign. Learn what the float test really means and how freshness differs from safety.
seo.search_intent: Recognize egg spoilage and understand the water-float test.

excerpt: A spoiled egg usually gives itself away with a strong unpleasant odor after cracking. The float test mainly indicates age because the air cell grows over time; it does not certify safety.
content_html:
The clearest household sign of a spoiled egg appears after cracking it: a strong, unpleasant odor. The popular float test tells you mostly about age because an egg's air cell grows as moisture and gases escape through the shell.

What the main signs mean

SignMeaning
Rotten or strongly off odor after crackingDiscard
Clearly abnormal appearanceMay indicate spoilage
Cracked or leaking shellHigher contamination concern
Egg floats in waterLarger air cell and older age
Thin, runny whiteLower freshness, not automatically spoilage

Smell

A spoiled egg develops a characteristic off odor whether raw or cooked. If you are unsure about an older egg, crack it into a small separate bowl before adding it to a batter or pan with other eggs.

There is no need to taste it. A clearly bad smell is enough reason to throw it away.

What the float test actually shows

As an egg ages, its air cell becomes larger. A very fresh egg tends to sink and lie flat; an older egg may stand upright; an egg with a large enough air cell can float.

USDA notes that a floating egg can still be usable. The test does not detect Salmonella or other pathogens.

Runny whites and flatter yolks

Fresh egg whites are usually thicker. As an egg ages, the white becomes more fluid and spreads farther in a pan. That is a change in freshness and cooking quality, not an automatic sign of dangerous spoilage.

Yolk color

A deep orange yolk is not proof of freshness, and a pale yolk is not a spoilage sign. Color depends mainly on pigments in the hen's diet.

Blood spots

Small blood spots can result from a tiny ruptured vessel during egg formation. They do not mean the egg is fertilized or rotten and can be removed for appearance if desired.

The shell matters

An intact shell is a protective barrier. An egg that has been cracked and leaking for an unknown amount of time creates more opportunity for contamination than one cracked immediately before cooking.

Can a normal-smelling egg contain Salmonella?

Yes. Pathogens do not have to create an odor. Storage, handling and cooking still matter even when an egg smells normal.

Refrigerator storage in the U.S.

USDA recommends refrigerating shell eggs and lists a typical refrigerator storage time of 3–5 weeks from purchase. Hard-cooked eggs keep about 1 week.

Bottom line

Use odor after cracking as the strongest spoilage clue. Use the float test as an age clue, not a safety test. A floating egg may still be usable, and a sinking egg is not guaranteed pathogen-free.

Sources

Guidance comes from USDA FSIS — Shell Eggs from Farm to Table and FoodSafety.gov.

faq.question: If an egg floats, is it bad?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Floating means the air cell has grown with age. Crack it into a separate bowl and check odor and appearance.

faq.question: How does a bad egg smell?
faq.answer: A spoiled egg develops a strong unpleasant odor that is usually obvious once cracked.

faq.question: How long do eggs keep in the refrigerator?
faq.answer: USDA lists 3–5 weeks for raw shell eggs in the refrigerator and about 1 week for hard-cooked eggs.
